DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
The pricing arithmetic is correct, and the price increases are defensible. But two of the paper's key claims are wrong or unsupported, and the projection leaves out costs the paper itself mentions.

## What checks out

- **Table 1.** Every margin is correct ((price − food cost) / price), and plates total 1,050.
- **The £810 projection.** 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2 = £810 a week, and × 52 = £42,120.
- **Competitor midpoints.** All three new prices are below the midpoint of the competitor range: fish £17.50 vs £17.98, burger £16.00 vs £16.50, steak £28.00 vs £29.50.
- **Main-course margin.** Moving to about 71% is right if volumes hold and costs don't change.

## Main problems

**1. The risotto has the strongest percentage margin on the menu, not the weakest.** Table 1 shows it at 80%, the highest of any dish. The weakest is the steak at 60%. Its sales (90 a week) tie with the specials rather than being uniquely lowest. Its cash profit per plate (£11.20) is above the burger (£10.80) and curry (£10.90).

Replacing it with a special at the same price will probably lower margin. Current specials run at 64%. At that rate a £14 special costs about £5.04 a plate against £2.80, which is about **£200 a week less** gross profit. The risotto may also be the only vegetarian main, and one vegetarian in a group can decide where the whole table eats. The paper's reason for removing it is contradicted by its own table. That doesn't rule out changing the dish, but any replacement should be costed to at least an 80% margin.

**2. The projection ignores the beef increase.** Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day as the new prices, but Section 5.3 assumes food costs stay flat. Applying 12% to the whole plate cost as an upper bound:

| Dish | Extra cost per plate | Plates per week | Extra cost per week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Steak | +£1.25 | 120 | £150 |
| Burger | +£0.50 | 260 | £131 |
| **Total** | | | **up to ~£280** |

Beef is only part of each plate's cost, so the real figure is somewhat lower. Even so, much of the burger and steak price rise just covers the beef increase.

**3. VAT.** UK menu prices include 20% VAT, and at roughly £900k a year in main-course sales the restaurant is certainly VAT-registered. A £1 price rise yields about £0.83 to the business, so the £810 is really about **£675 a week net**. The margins in Table 1 are also calculated on VAT-inclusive prices; on a net basis fish and chips is about 63%, not 69%. Before comparing anything with the 70% target, it's worth confirming which basis that target uses.

**Putting 1–3 together**, with volumes holding:

| | £ per week |
|---|---|
| Price rises, net of VAT | ≈ +675 |
| Beef increase | up to −280 |
| Risotto swap, if the special runs at 64% | ≈ −200 |
| **Net change** | **≈ +£200–300** |

That is roughly £10–16k a year, not £42k. Main-course margin would end up at or below where it is now, not at 71%.

**4. "Volumes will hold" is assumed, not shown.** The new prices break even if sales of each dish fall by about:

| Dish | Break-even volume fall |
|---|---|
| Fish and chips | 8% |
| Burger | 8–9% |
| Steak | 11% |

These figures ignore beef and VAT, which would make the margin for error smaller. Some guests who switch to the curry or another dish aren't lost, which softens this.

The evidence offered for loyalty is weak:
- A 60% repeat rate shows loyalty, not price insensitivity. Regulars are the guests most likely to notice the change.
- "No visible effect on bookings" in 2024 is a measure of bookings, not plates sold.
- The paper calls weekday lunch trade "a small share," but the data say only that Friday and Saturday dinner make up just under half. The lunch share isn't given. Burgers and fish and chips are probably lunch staples.

**5. The monitoring plan can't detect a price effect.** Comparing April and May with January and February will show a seasonal rise regardless, and Easter falls on 5 April 2026. That could easily hide a 5–10% drop caused by the price change. A fairer baseline is the same weeks in 2025, or tracking each dish's share of covers. The plan also sets no threshold for what counts as an early warning, or what happens if one is triggered.

## Smaller points

- **Trading days.** The Recommendation says "six trading days a week," but Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **Annualisation.** Multiplying January–February weekly figures by 52 assumes those weeks are typical and that the restaurant never closes. Both are worth stating.

## On the author's description

- **"Remain the value option."** The paper itself says only "below the midpoint," which is accurate. After the changes the restaurant would no longer be cheapest on any of the three dishes: competitors offer fish at £16.95, burgers at £15.50 and steak at £27.00.
- **"Latest supplier information."** The supplier information is in the paper but isn't used in the projection.
- **The menu-mix decision is "clear-cut."** It is, but in the opposite direction from the one proposed.

## Suggested changes before it goes to the owners

1. Keep the risotto, or replace it only with a dish costed at 80% or better.
2. Re-run the projection net of VAT, including the beef increase, and show the break-even volume falls.
3. Consider whether the burger and steak increases need to be higher to absorb beef, or whether part of the increase should move to the curry, which is not priced against competitors.
4. Monitor against the same weeks in 2025, with a stated trigger for review.

Raising prices on these three dishes is still a reasonable move. The case for it just needs to rest on about £15k a year, not £42k.
